text: The Southern Baptist Convention (SBC), also known as the Great Commission Baptists (GCB), is a Christian denomination based in the United States and is the world's largest Baptist organization, the largest Protestant denomination, and the second-largest Christian body in the U.S. It consists of fully autonomous, independent churches that share common essential beliefs and pool resources for missions. Churches are evangelical, emphasizing individual conversion, which is affirmed through complete immersion baptism—a public, symbolic act representing burial of the old life and resurrection to new life, not a requirement for salvation. The denomination maintains a male pastorate, citing 1 Timothy 2:12, and denies the legitimacy of same-sex marriage, asserting that marriage is exclusively between a man and a woman and that all sexual relations must occur within marriage. Beliefs vary by congregation due to local autonomy. In 1845, Southern Baptists split from the Triennial Convention to support slavery, as American society divided over the issue preceding the Civil War. In 1995, the SBC apologized for its historical racial positions, and today it is racially diverse, with one in four congregations having a nonwhite majority. Since the 1940s, it has expanded across the U.S., with tens of thousands of affiliated churches and 41 state conventions. A conservative movement gained control of the SBC leadership by the 1990s. Self-reported membership peaked in 2006 at about 16 million, declined by an estimated 13.6% since then, with 2020 marking the 14th year of continuous decline, and weekly attendance dropped about 27% between 2006 and 2020. In 2024, the convention reported increased participation and a slowing of membership decline, with 12,722,266 members. The name "Southern" originates from the 1845 founding in Augusta, Georgia, by white Baptists who supported slavery and separated from northern Baptists, who opposed funding evangelists involved in slavery. In 2012, the SBC adopted the descriptor "Great Commission Baptists" after electing its first African American president, and in 2020, some leaders proposed changing the name to distance it from its white supremacist origins and reflect its no longer being a specifically Southern church; some affiliated churches have also adopted the descriptor. Early Baptists in British colonies came from England in the 17th century due to dissent from the Church of England. Roger Williams founded the first Baptist church in British America in 1638 in Providence Plantations, Rhode Island. The oldest Baptist church in the South, First Baptist Church of Charleston, South Carolina, was organized in 1682 by William Screven. Baptist churches were formed in Virginia in 1715 through Robert Norden and in North Carolina in 1727 through Paul Palmer. Baptists followed a congregational polity, operating independently of the state-established Anglican churches in the South, where non-Anglicans were barred from political office. By 1740, there were about eight Baptist churches in Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina with 300 to 400 members. New members, both black and white, were converted by Baptist preachers during the 18th and 19th centuries, especially during the First and Second Great Awakenings. Black churches were founded in Virginia, South Carolina, and Georgia before the American Revolution, and some maintained independence after Nat Turner's Rebellion of 1831. Before the Revolution, Baptist and Methodist evangelicals promoted the equality of all people before God, including enslaved people and free blacks, challenging class and racial hierarchies and urging planters to abolish slavery. There was a divide between the plain-living, common-people-oriented Baptists and the opulent, slave-owning Anglican gentry, who viewed Baptist discipline as radical but saw it as a way to maintain order. Baptists strictly monitored moral conduct, expelling members for sexual transgressions, cursing, or excessive drinking. In Virginia and other southern colonies, the Church of England was the established church and opposed Baptist growth, prosecuting preachers for "disturbing the peace" and having them defended by Patrick Henry and James Madison. In 1779, Thomas Jefferson wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, enacted in 1786, and James Madison later incorporated religious freedom into the U.S. Constitution. The struggle for religious tolerance intensified during the American Revolution, with Baptists opposing the Anglican establishment, and the conflict between evangelical and gentry styles becoming bitter. In 1814, leaders like Luther Rice helped unify Baptists nationally under the Triennial Convention, which met every three years and supported missions abroad. The Home Mission Society, established in 1832, supported missions in U.S. frontier territories. By the mid-19th century, social, cultural, economic, and political differences emerged between northern, western, and southern groups, with slavery being the most divisive issue, followed by missions. Northern Baptists, along with Quakers and Methodists, increasingly argued that enslavers must free enslaved people during the Second Great Awakening. While most southern Baptists were yeomen and common planters, many attracted major planters who interpreted the Bible as supporting slavery and encouraged paternalistic practices. They preached to enslaved people to accept their status and obey enslavers and welcomed enslaved people and free blacks as members, though whites controlled leadership and often segregated seating. In 1821, Gillfield Baptist in Petersburg, Virginia, had the largest congregation in the Portsmouth Association with 441 members, more than twice the size of the next-largest church. Before 1831, Gillfield had a black preacher; after Nat Turner's Rebellion, the state required white men to oversee black congregations, and Gillfield could not appoint a black preacher until after the Civil War and emancipation. After the rebellion, whites passed laws requiring white ministers to lead or be present at meetings, and many enslaved people evaded these restrictions. The Triennial Convention and the Home Mission Society maintained neutrality on slavery, refusing to endorse or condemn it. In 1844, during the "Georgia Test Case," the Georgia State Convention proposed appointing enslaver Elder James E. Reeve as a missionary, but the Foreign Mission Board refused, citing neutrality. In 1844, University of Alabama president Basil Manly Sr., who enslaved 40 people, drafted the "Alabama Resolutions" demanding that enslavers be eligible for denominational offices, which were not adopted. Many southern Baptists tested neutrality by recommending an enslaver to the Home Mission Society, which refused, noting missionaries could not take servants and would not appear to endorse slavery. Many southerners viewed the northern stance that "slaveholding brethren were less than followers of Jesus" as a justification for seceding. This conflict culminated in 1845 when northern representatives refused to appoint missionaries whose families enslaved people, leading many southern Baptists to split and form the Southern Baptist Convention. A secondary concern was that the American Baptist Home Mission Society did not appoint a sufficient number of missionaries to the South, likely due to not appointing enslavers. Northern Baptists favored a loose structure with individual annual dues and single-ministry societies, while southern Baptists preferred a centralized, association-based structure with multiple ministries under one organization. Increasing tensions and southern discontent over criticism of slavery and mission policies led to their withdrawal from national Baptist organizations. The Southern Baptists met in May 1845 at the First Baptist Church of Augusta and formed the Southern Baptist Convention, electing William Bullein Johnson as its first president, who had previously served as president of the Triennial Convention in 1841. African Americans founded churches early on, such as in Petersburg, Virginia (1774) and Savannah, Georgia (1788), and later in frontier areas like First African Baptist Church of Lexington, Kentucky, which joined the Elkhorn Association in 1824 and had 1,820 members by 1850 and 2,223 by 1861. Southern whites generally required black churches to have white ministers and trustees, with segregated seating, and white preaching often emphasized that enslaved people should accept their place and behave well toward enslavers. After the Civil War, freedmen formed independent black congregations, regional associations, and state and national conventions, seeking independence from white supervision. They saw their liberation as analogous to the Exodus and viewed John Brown as their Moses. In 1866, black Baptists formed the Consolidated American Baptist Convention, and in 1895, they merged three national conventions to create the National Baptist Convention, USA, which now has over eight million members and is the largest African American religious organization, second only to the Southern Baptists. Free black people in the North founded independent churches in the early 19th century. During Reconstruction, missionaries from northern denominations, especially the African Methodist Episcopal Church, attracted tens and hundreds of thousands of freedmen, leading many white Southern Baptist churches to lose black members to new denominations and independent congregations. During the civil rights movement, many Southern Baptist pastors and members rejected racial integration and upheld white supremacy, further alienating African Americans. Historian Wayne Flynt described the church as "the last bastion of segregation," and the SBC did not integrate seminary classrooms until 1951. In 1995, the SBC voted to adopt a resolution renouncing its racist roots and apologizing for its past defense of slavery, segregation, and white supremacy, marking its first formal acknowledgment of racism's role in its history. By the early 21st century, ethnically diverse congregations were increasing, with nearly 20% of congregations being majority African American, Asian, Hispanic, or Latino in 2008, and an estimated one million African American members in cooperating churches. The SBC has passed resolutions recommending greater inclusion of black members and appointing more African American leaders. In 2012, it elected Pastor Fred Luter of the Franklin Avenue Baptist Church as its first African American president. In 2005, proposals to rename the SBC to "North American Baptist Convention" or "Scriptural Baptist Convention" were defeated. In 2012, messengers voted to adopt the descriptor "Great Commission Baptists," with the legal name remaining "Southern Baptist Convention," though affiliated churches and entities could voluntarily use it. Almost a year after the Charleston church shooting, the denomination approved a resolution urging member churches and families to stop flying the Confederate flag. It also approved a resolution, "On Refugee Ministry," encouraging churches and families to welcome refugees. Russell Moore of the Southern Baptist Ethics and Religious Liberty Commission responded to a pastor's question about supporting Muslim mosque construction by stating that religious freedom must be for all religions and that such questions are not simple. From February to June 2016, the SBC collaborated with the National Baptist Convention, USA, on racial reconciliation, with presidents Ronnie Floyd and Jerry Young assembling ten pastors from each convention to discuss race relations; in 2016, Baptist Press and The New York Times reported tension within the National Baptist Convention, with President Jerry Young stating that while he understood the history and pain of slavery, he saw it as reverse racism to oppose collaboration, emphasizing that the Gospel demands reconciliation. After an initial resolution against the alt-right failed to pass, the denomination officially denounced the alt-right at its 2017 convention. On November 5, 2017, a mass shooting occurred at the First Baptist Church of Sutherland Springs, the deadliest shooting at any affiliated church in its history and the deadliest at an American place of worship in modern times. In 2020, the denomination canceled its convention due to COVID-19 concerns.

Fellowship members in the same denomination contacted Dr. Jerry Young, asking, "What are you doing? I mean, are you not aware of the history?" He responded that he is fully aware of the history and the pain associated with it, but emphasized that from his perspective, using the history of slavery as a reason to avoid involvement with the Southern Baptists is reverse racism. He affirmed that if the Gospel is to have any effect, it must demand that we not only preach but also practice reconciliation. In 2017, after an initial resolution denouncing the alt-right movement failed to reach the convention floor, the Southern Baptist Convention officially condemned the alt-right at its convention. On November 5, 2017, a mass shooting occurred at the First Baptist Church of Sutherland Springs, which was the deadliest shooting at any affiliated church in its history and the deadliest at an American place of worship in modern times. In 2020, the denomination canceled its convention due to COVID-19 concerns and rescheduled it for June 2021. In a September 15, 2020, Washington Post story, J. D. Greear stated that some SBC leaders wanted to rename the church "Great Commission Baptists" to distance it from its historical ties to slavery and to reflect that it is no longer solely a Southern church; since then, several churches have adopted this alternative name. In 2018, investigations revealed that the SBC suppressed reports of sexual abuse and protected over 700 accused ministers and church workers. In 2022, a report found that church leaders had stonewalled and disparaged survivors of clergy sexual abuse for nearly two decades; reform efforts were criticized or dismissed by other leaders; and known abusers were allowed to retain their positions without informing their local churches. On August 12, 2022, the denomination announced it was facing a federal investigation into the abuse scandal. A joint investigation by the Houston Chronicle and the San Antonio Express in 2019 found over 700 victims of sexual abuse by nearly 400 church leaders, pastors, and volunteers over 20 years. The Chronicle examined federal and state court databases, prison records, and official documents from over 20 states and sex offender registries nationwide, compiling a list of pastors, leaders, employees, and volunteers convicted or who pleaded guilty to sex crimes as of June 2019. On June 12, 2019, during its annual meeting in Birmingham, Alabama, convention messengers approved a resolution condemning sex abuse and establishing a special committee to investigate it and to make it easier for the convention to excommunicate churches. Reverend J. D. Greear called it a "defining moment," and Ronnie Floyd, president of the executive committee, called it a "very, very significant moment in the history of the Southern Baptist Convention." In June 2021, leaked letters from former policy director Russell D. Moore to convention leadership revealed that the convention had mishandled claims of sexual abuse. On May 22, 2022, Guidepost Solutions, an independent firm hired by the executive committee, released a report detailing that church leaders had stonewalled and disparaged survivors for nearly two decades, spending $4 million on the inquiry; it also found that known abusers were allowed to keep their positions without informing their churches. The report noted that although Greear, elected president in 2018, made addressing sexual abuse a central agenda, nearly all reform efforts were met with criticism and dismissal by other leaders. On June 14, 2022, the denomination voted to create a system to track pastors and other church workers credibly accused of sex abuse and to launch a new task force to oversee further reforms after a consultant revealed that leaders had mishandled abuse cases and stonewalled victims for years. The task force will operate for one year, with the option to continue. On August 12, 2022, the organization announced it was facing a federal investigation into the sex abuse scandal. As abuse revelations and lawsuits continued into 2023, the SBC's Abuse Reform Implementation Task Force announced ongoing development of a database of sexual offenders. The Baptist Faith and Message (BF&M) represents the general theological perspective of the denomination's churches. The convention first drafted the BF&M in 1925 as a revision of the 1833 New Hampshire Confession of Faith, revised it significantly in 1963, amended it in 1998 to add a section on the family, and revised it again in 2000. The 1998 and 2000 changes sparked controversy, especially regarding women's roles in the church. The BF&M is not a creed like the Nicene Creed; members are not required to adhere to it, and churches or state conventions are not required to use it as their statement of faith, though many do. However, key leaders, faculty in denomination-owned seminaries, and missionaries applying through missionary agencies must affirm that their practices, doctrine, and preaching are consistent with the BF&M. In 2012, a LifeWay Research survey found that 30% of churches identified as Calvinist or Reformed, and 30% as Arminian or Wesleyan; Ed Stetzer noted that historically many Baptists have considered themselves neither, holding a unique theological approach. The survey also found that 60% of pastors were concerned about Calvinism's influence within the convention. Nathan Finn noted that the debate over Calvinism has intensified, with non-Calvinists especially concerned about Founders Ministries and Calvinists especially concerned about revivalism and Keswick theology. Historically, the denomination has not considered glossolalia or other Charismatic beliefs to be in accordance with Scriptural teaching, though the BF&M does not mention it. In 2015, the International Mission Board lifted a ban on glossolalia for its missionaries while reaffirming it should not be taught as normative. The convention brings together fundamentalist and moderate churches. In addition to the BF&M, the denomination has issued position statements affirming the autonomy of the local church, the importance of the Cooperative Program of missions, that statements of belief are revisable in light of Scripture though the Bible is the final word, honoring the indigenous principle in missions without compromising doctrine, that laypersons have the same right as ordained ministers to communicate with God, interpret Scripture, and minister in Christ's name, that at the moment of conception a new being enters the universe, created in God's image, and should be protected regardless of circumstances, that God's plan for marriage and sexual intimacy is a lifelong relationship of one man and one woman, rejecting homosexuality, and that the Bible forbids any form of extramarital sexual relations, affirming individual accountability before God, and that women are not eligible to serve as pastors. In 2022, the convention passed a resolution against prosperity theology, which it considers a heretical distortion of the Bible. The denomination's position on abortion has changed significantly over time, evolving from acceptance under certain circumstances to firm opposition. In 1971, the SBC passed a resolution urging a loosening of U.S. abortion laws, calling for legislation allowing abortion in cases of rape, incest, severe fetal deformity, or when a mother's emotional, mental, or physical health is at risk. In 1973, a Baptist Standard poll found that 90% of Texas Baptists believed their state's abortion laws were too restrictive. During this era, a majority of Southern Baptists, including some conservatives, supported a moderate expansion of abortion rights, viewing it as a matter of religious liberty, lacking biblical condemnation, and believing in non-intrusive government. Their initial reaction to Roe v. Wade was support or indifference, seeing anti-abortion movements as sectarian and Catholic. By the mid-1970s, this began to shift, and the movement to change Southern Baptist opinions on abortion substantially influenced their views. Over time, the SBC changed, and today it strongly opposes abortion. The denomination officially subscribes to a complementarian view of gender roles. Beginning in the early 1970s, as a reaction to women's liberation movements, the church and other historically conservative Baptist groups began asserting traditional gender roles. In 1973, at the annual meeting, delegates passed a resolution stating, "Man was not made for woman, but the woman for the man. Woman is the glory of man. Woman would not have existed without man." In 1998, the convention added a male leadership understanding of marriage to the 1963 BF&M with an official amendment: Article XVIII, "The Family." In 2000, it revised the document to support a male-only pastorate with no mention of the office of deacon. In 1984, when there were about 250 women pastors, the convention adopted a resolution affirming the exclusion of women from pastoral leadership. Since 1987, local associations and regional conventions have considered churches that authorize women as pastors to be not in friendly cooperation (or "disfellowshipped") without national convention intervention. By explicitly defining the pastoral office as the exclusive domain of males, the 2000 BF&M became the denomination's first official position against women pastors. Because individual churches are autonomous, they cannot be forced to adopt a male-only pastorate. Some churches that have appointed women as pastors have been disfellowshipped from local associations; a smaller number from state conventions. In February 2023, the Executive Committee first deemed five churches that had appointed women pastors to not be in friendly cooperation. In June 2023, when two churches requested a review, 88% of convention representatives voted to uphold the decision. American Reformer magazine estimated the convention would have 1,844 female pastors in 2023. The crystallization of the church's positions on gender roles and restrictions on women's pastoral roles contributed to the split of members joining the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship, which broke from the convention in 1991. The Alliance of Baptists also accepts women's ordination. The 2000 BF&M prescribes a husband-headship authority structure, closely following a complementarian reading of Paul's exhortations in Ephesians 5:21–33. Article XVIII. The Family. The husband and wife are of equal worth before God, both created in God's image. The marriage relationship models how God relates to His people. A husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church, has the God-given responsibility to provide for, protect, and lead his family. A wife is to submit graciously to her husband's servant leadership, even as the church submits to Christ's headship; she, being in God's image as is her husband, has the God-given responsibility to respect her husband and serve as his helper in managing the household and nurturing the next generation. Southern/Great Commission Baptists observe two ordinances: the Lord's Supper and believer's baptism (also known as credo-baptism, from the Latin for "I believe"). They hold the historic Baptist belief that immersion is the only valid mode of baptism. The BF&M describes baptism as a symbolic act of obedience and a testimony of the believer's faith in Jesus Christ to others and notes that it is a precondition to congregational church membership. The BF&M holds to memorialism, the belief that the Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience in which believers commemorate Christ's death and look forward to His Second Coming. Individual churches are free to practice open or closed communion due to the convention's belief in congregational polity and local church autonomy, though most practice open communion. The frequency of the Lord's Supper varies; churches commonly observe it quarterly, some monthly, and a small minority weekly. Because the organization traditionally opposes alcoholic beverage consumption, grape juice is used instead of wine. Most members observe a low church form of worship, less formal and without a stated liturgy. The form of worship depends on whether the congregation uses traditional or contemporary services or a mix of both—main differences are in music and the response to the sermon. In both types, there is a prayer at the beginning, before the sermon, and at the end. Offerings are taken, either mid-service or at the end; with the rise of electronic systems, some churches offer online or app-based giving. Responsive Scripture readings are uncommon but may occur on special occasions. In a traditional service, music typically features hymns with piano or organ (churches have generally phased out organ due to changing preferences), sometimes with a soloist or choir. Smaller churches allow anyone to participate in the choir regardless of singing ability; larger churches limit participation to those who have successfully tried out. After the sermon, an invitation to respond (sometimes called an altar call) may be given; people may respond by receiving Christ as Lord and Savior, beginning discipleship, seeking baptism, joining the congregation, or entering vocational ministry. Churches may schedule baptisms on specific weekends or offer them when a baptistry is available. In a contemporary service, music generally features modern songs led by a praise team or similar group with featured singers; choirs are less common. An altar call may or may not be given; if not, interested persons are directed to the lobby to speak with someone. Baptismal services are usually scheduled as special events. Church membership is typically done through periodic classes on church history, beliefs, goals, and expectations. Controversially, churches may require a member to sign a "membership covenant," a document with promises such as regular attendance, regular giving (sometimes including tithing), and service within the church. Such covenants are controversial because they may not allow a member to withdraw voluntarily from membership or, in some cases, to leave at all without leadership approval. A Dallas/Fort Worth church was forced to apologize to a member who attempted to annul her marriage after her husband admitted to viewing child pornography. According to a 2024 census published by the convention, it had 46,876 churches, 4.3 million weekly worshippers, and 12,722,266 members. The global convention has more than 1,161 local associations, 41 state conventions, and fellowships covering all 50 states and territories of the United States.

A prospective member of the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC) may be asked to sign a "membership covenant," a document outlining commitments such as regular attendance at main services and small groups, consistent giving—sometimes including tithing—and service within the church. These covenants are controversial because they may restrict a member’s ability to voluntarily withdraw from membership to avoid church discipline, or in some cases, prevent leaving the church entirely without leadership approval. For example, a Dallas/Fort Worth church was forced to apologize when a member attempted to annul her marriage after her husband admitted to viewing child pornography, as the church had not requested permission for the annulment. According to a 2024 census, the SBC comprises 46,876 churches, 4.3 million weekly worshippers, and 12,722,266 members. The global convention includes more than 1,161 local associations, 41 state conventions, and fellowships covering all 50 U.S. states and territories. The states with the highest membership rates are Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, Florida, and Tennessee, with Texas having the largest number of members—estimated at 2.75 million—divided between the more traditionalist Southern Baptists of Texas Convention and the more moderate, diversified Baptist General Convention of Texas, which is more financially and organizationally autonomous than most state conventions. Southern/Great Commission Baptists support thousands of missionaries through the Cooperative Program. Data from church sources and independent surveys show that since 1990, SBC membership as a proportion of the American population has declined. The convention grew historically until 2007, when membership decreased by nearly 40,000, with total membership at about 16.2 million remaining flat over the period, falling by 38,482 or 0.2%. New baptisms have declined annually for seven of the last eight years, reaching their lowest levels since 1987 by 2008, and continued to decline through 2012. The 2014 statistical summary recorded a loss of 236,467 members, the largest one-year decline since 1881, and by 2018, membership fell below 15 million for the first time since 1989, reaching its lowest level in over 30 years. This decline has led some researchers to describe the SBC as a "denomination in decline," with former president Frank Page suggesting in 2008 that half of the convention’s churches could close permanently by 2030. A 2004 survey found that 70% of SBC churches had declining or plateaued membership. The decline is attributed to four factors: increased immigration by non-European groups, stagnant growth among predominantly European American churches, the aging of current members, and reduced participation by younger generations. Some believe Baptists have not sufficiently attracted minorities, though state conventions in Mississippi and Texas report rising minority membership. In 1990, 5% of congregations were non-white; by 2012, that proportion had risen to 20%, with 60% of minority congregations located in Texas, especially in Houston and Dallas suburbs. By 2020, an estimated 22.3% of affiliated churches were non-white. The decline may be more significant than statistics suggest because churches are not required to remove inactive members, leading to inflated numbers, and hundreds of moderate congregations have shifted allegiance to other Baptist groups like the American Baptist Churches USA, the Alliance of Baptists, or the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship while remaining on the SBC’s rolls. Groups have withdrawn due to conservative trends; for instance, in 2000, the Baptist General Convention of Texas cut contributions to Southern Baptist seminaries and redirected over $5 million to more moderate seminaries, including the Hispanic Baptist Theological School in San Antonio, Baylor’s George W. Truett Theological Seminary in Waco, and Hardin–Simmons’ Logsdon School of Theology in Abilene. Since the 1980s controversies, the convention has established over 20 theological programs for moderate and progressive Baptists in the Southeast, including in Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina, and Alabama. Texas and Virginia have the largest state conventions with moderate theological approaches. On June 4, 2020, the SBC reported a 13th consecutive year of membership decline, dropping nearly 2% to 14,525,579 from 2018 to 2019, and in 2022 lost 457,371 members—its largest drop in over a century—to 13,223,122, a level similar to the late 1970s. The denomination has four organizational levels: local congregation, local association, state convention, and national convention, with 41 affiliated state conventions or fellowships. Churches voluntarily pool resources through cooperative associations to support missionary and other work, but the national convention, state conventions, and local associations have no administrative or ecclesiastical control over local churches; they may disfellowship a congregation on an issue but cannot terminate leadership, members, or force closure. The national convention does not claim authority over any other Baptist body, as stated in Article IV. Authority. The national convention maintains a central administrative office in Nashville, Tennessee, where its executive committee controls seminaries and other institutions. As of 2008, the denomination had around 10,000 ethnic churches. The executive committee rejected a proposal to create a convention-wide database of clergy accused of sexual crimes due to the principle of local church autonomy. A 2009 Lifeway Christian Resources study found that one in eight background checks for church workers revealed a history of crime that could have prevented them from working. The Baptist Faith and Message is not binding on churches or members, though national employees and missionaries must agree to it. Southern/Great Commission Baptists are generally conservative, opposing homosexual activity and abortion. Baptists recognize only two scriptural offices: pastor-teacher and deacon, with a 1980s resolution officially restricting ordained offices to men, based on New Testament scriptures. The annual meeting, held in June over two days, includes delegates ("messengers") from cooperating churches who determine programs, policies, and budgets, elect officers, and committees. Each church may send up to two messengers, with a maximum of 12. The Cooperative Program (CP) collects and distributes funds from congregations to support regional, national, and international ministries. In the fiscal year ending September 30, 2008, local congregations reported $11.1 billion in gift receipts, sending $548 million—about 5%—to state conventions via the CP, of which $344 million was retained by state conventions and $204 million went to the national CP. The denomination was founded in 1845 to establish a mission board. The North American Mission Board (NAMB) in Alpharetta, Georgia, supports missionaries in the U.S. and Canada, while the International Mission Board (IMB) in Richmond, Virginia, supports missionaries worldwide. Baptist Men is the mission organization for men under NAMB. The Woman's Missionary Union, founded in 1888, supports two major annual missions: the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering and the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering. Southern Baptist Disaster Relief, initiated in 1967, responded to 166 named disasters in 2005, preparing 17,124,738 meals, repairing 7,246 homes, and removing debris from 13,986 yards. The organization provides free, essential services such as food, water, child care, and rebuilding. The SBC has affiliated primary and secondary schools and universities. The national convention directly supports six theological seminaries. Other notable organizations include Baptist Press (founded 1946), Baptist Collegiate Network, GuideStone Financial Resources (founded 1918), LifeWay Christian Resources (founded 1891), the Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission, and the Southern Baptist Historical Library and Archives in Nashville. The SBC has experienced major internal controversies, including Landmarkism in the 1850s–1860s, which led to the formation of the American Baptist Association and many independent churches. The Whitsitt controversy (1896–99) challenged the timeline of Baptist immersion. From the 19th to 20th century, the SBC supported white supremacy, racial segregation, the Confederacy, and opposed interracial marriage. A conservative movement gained control from the late 1970s onward, culminating in 1995 when the SBC officially denounced racism. In the 21st century, after electing its first Black president, the SBC adopted the "Great Commission Baptists" descriptor to distance itself from its white supremacist past. By 2008, nearly 20% of SBC congregations were majority African American, Asian, Hispanic, or Latino, with an estimated one million African American members. By 2018, the denomination passed resolutions to increase black membership and appoint more African American leaders. The Southern Baptist Convention conservative resurgence (c. 1970–2000) was a struggle for control of resources and ideology. In 1961, Professor Ralph Elliott published a book rejecting biblical inerrancy. In the 1970s, other seminary professors were criticized for liberal views. In response, a group led by Judge Paul Pressler and Pastor Paige Patterson campaigned for a conservative direction, resulting in Adrian Rogers being elected president in 1979. New leaders replaced all agency heads with more conservative individuals, a move called the "conservative resurgence" by supporters and "fundamentalist takeover" by opponents. Russell H. Dilday described the resurgence as a "self-destructive, contentious, one-sided feud." In 1984, a resolution was passed excluding women from pastoral leadership. In 1987, churches opposed to fundamentalist control founded the Alliance of Baptists; in 1991, moderate churches formed the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship over similar concerns.

From 1978 to 1994, the resurgence fragmented Southern Baptist fellowship and was described as "far more serious than [a controversy]" and a "self-destructive, contentious, one-sided feud that at times took on combative characteristics." Since 1979, Southern Baptists had become polarized into two major groups: moderates and conservatives. Reflecting the conservative majority votes of messengers at the 1979 annual meeting of the SBC, the new national organization officers replaced all leaders of Southern Baptist agencies with presumably more conservative individuals, often labeled "fundamentalist" by dissenters. In 1984, this group passed a resolution excluding women from pastoral leadership. In 1987, a group of churches criticized the fundamentalists for controlling leadership and founded the Alliance of Baptists. A group of moderate churches also criticized the denomination for leadership control and opposition to women's ministry, and founded the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship in 1991. In 2019, after sexual abuse scandals involving deacon Paul Pressler and cover-ups involving former president Paige Patterson, Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary removed the stained-glass windows from the MacGorman Chapel opened in 2011 that depicted them as actors of a "conservative resurgence." Since 1976, the Convention has adopted 22 resolutions supporting only marriage between a man and a woman and opposing same-sex marriage. Since 1992, the national convention has "disfellowshipped" various churches that support LGBTQ inclusion; in 2018, the District of Columbia Baptist Convention was disfellowshipped for this reason. On June 10, 2025, at the annual meeting in Dallas, the convention voted overwhelmingly in favor of working to overturn the legal right to same-sex marriage, marking the first time the SBC had asked its member churches to do so. The resolution also opposed "transgender ideology." The resolution, "On Restoring Moral Clarity through God's Design for Gender, Marriage, and the Family," was written by Andrew T. Walker, an ethicist at a Kentucky seminary. By November 2020, the six convention seminary presidents called critical race theory "unbiblical," emphasizing the importance of not turning to secular ideas to confront racism; four African American churches left the SBC over the leadership's charged statement on the issue.
